# Human trust in otherware – a systematic literature review bringing all antecedents together

Till Saßmannshausen<sup>a</sup> , Peter Burggr€af<sup>a</sup> , Marc Hassenzahl<sup>b</sup> and Johannes Wagner<sup>a</sup>

<sup>a</sup>Chair of International Production Engineering and Management, University of Siegen, Siegen, Germany; <sup>b</sup>Chair of Ubiquitous Design, University of Siegen, Siegen, Germany

## ABSTRACT

Technological systems are becoming increasingly smarter, which causes a shift in the way they are seen: from tools used to execute specific tasks to social counterparts with whom to cooperate. To ensure that these interactions are successful, trust has proven to be the most important driver. We conducted an extensive and structured review with the goal to reveal all previously researched antecedents influencing the human trust in technology-based counterparts. In doing so, we synthesised 179 papers and uncovered 479 trust antecedents. We assigned these antecedents to four main groups. Three of them have been explored before: environment, trustee, and trustor. Within this paper, we argue for a fourth group, the interaction. This quadripartition allows the inclusion of antecedents that were not considered previously. Moreover, we critically question the practice of uncovering more and more trust antecedents, which already led to an opaque plethora and thus becomes increasingly complex for practitioners.

**ARTICLE HISTORY** Received 5 November 2021 Accepted 28 August 2022

**KEYWORDS** Artificial intelligence; automation; robot; interaction; teaming

**Practitioner summary:** Future designers of intelligent and interactive technology will have to consider trust to a greater extent. We emphasise that there are far more trust antecedents – and interdependencies – to consider than the ethically motivated discussions about “Trustworthy AI” suggest. For this purpose, we derived a trust map as a sound basis.

## Intelligent technology, a matter of trust

Intelligent technology is becoming smarter and increasingly integral to everyday life (Sethumadhavan 2019). The expectation is that this autonomous and mostly artificial intelligence-based technology is different from previous classic (rule-based) automation and thus will be able to master complex cognitive tasks and support decision-making (World Economic Forum 2015; McAfee and Brynjolfsson 2017). In fact, current successful applications of virtual assistants for managerial tasks, such as launching a new product, support this notion (Sowa, Przegalinska, and Ciechanowski 2021). It seems that using artificial intelligence (AI) for this kind of task, which is normally conducted by wellpaid knowledge workers and top managers, makes its use even more financially attractive for organisations (Glikson and Woolley 2020). Thus, AI is expected to fundamentally transform organisational structures (Davis 2019). For the management level of organisations, this transformation will lead to, what we call, cyber management. Here, human and artificial intelligence cooperate successfully as a team (Burggr€af, Wagner, and Saßmannshausen 2021).

This rise of AI spurred organisations and governments around the world to establish guidelines for developing, deploying, and using ethical, rightsrespecting, and socially beneficial AI (Fjeld et al. 2020). While these guidelines promote the terms trust or trustworthy, like the one of the European Commission (High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence 2019), they provide only ethical statements, such as the consideration of non-discrimination approaches (Toreini et al. 2019). Without questioning the usefulness of these guidelines, we want to point out that they employ the term trust in disregard of trust research (Sutrop 2019), because trust in AI does not necessarily depend on ethical considerations (Toreini et al. 2019).

From the perspective of trust research, Luhmann (1979, p. 16) predicted the growing importance of trust in technology more than 40 years ago: “one should expect trust to be increasingly in demand as a means of enduring the complexity of a future which technology will generate.” Since then, the question of trust in intelligent systems has been and is being investigated in several disciplines (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2018). For example, in autonomous driving, the vehicle’s behaviour should adapt based on the driver’s trust level (Xu and Dudek 2015). Health- and homecare applications attempt to create trust through transparency and adaptability (Rossi et al. 2017; Fischer, Weigelin, and Bodenhagen 2018). In safetycritical applications, such as airport security (Merritt et al. 2015), research focus on the effects of trust errors (Rovira, Pak, and McLaughlin 2017).

The broadly agreed aim for human-machine teams is the appropriate calibration of human trust (Hancock et al. 2011; de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018; Siau and Wang 2018). To prevent misuse, we have to avoid overtrust; to prevent disuse, we have to avoid undertrust (Parasuraman and Riley 1997; Lee and See 2004). In general, the technology is expected to be designed in a trust-building way. While some factors, aspects, attributions, or characteristics – or antecedents as we call them in this article – support trust-building, others diminish it. In recent years, research studied such influential trust antecedents in different forms of technology. Previous synthesising studies – mostly metaanalyses – solely included publications where trust and the effect of antecedents were measured quantitatively and the focus lied on specific forms of technology, like robots (Hancock et al. 2011; Hancock et al. 2021), automation (Hoff and Bashir 2013; Schaefer et al. 2016), or recently AI (Kaplan et al. 2021). In order to complement these rather specific studies, the goal of the present paper is to create a full picture of trust antecedents in the presence of intelligent – mostly AI-based – counterparts.

## Trust in technology, from tool to otherware

The concept of trust is an integral and ubiquitous element of everyday human-human interaction as well as, to some extent, of human-technology interaction. Yet, trust remains challenging to define and to study (Toreini et al. 2019). It has its origin in human-human relationships and is characterised as multidimensional, multidisciplinary, and multifaceted (Rousseau et al. 1998). Across different disciplines, such as philosophy, psychology, and economics (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2018), trust is variably understood as belief, attitude, or behaviour (Hoff and Bashir 2015; Guo and Yang 2020).

In researching trust in technology, two major questions emerge: First, is there such a thing as trust in technology at all, and second, is trust in technology similar to trust in humans? At the heart of both debates lies the same issue: humans are not machines. In the first debate, this obvious difference is used to fundamentally question the concept of trust in human-machine relationships (Schmidt, Biessmann, and Teubner 2020) and to promote the concept of reliance instead (Deley and Dubois 2020). In this view, trust remains a phenomenon reserved for humanhuman interactions. This inevitably leads to a discussion about the similarities and differences between trust and reliance (see for example Baier (1986), Holton (1994), and Sutrop (2019)). We follow Lee and See’s (2004, p. 51) notion that “Trust guides – but does not completely determine – reliance” (see also Muir and Moray (1996), Lewandowsky, Mundy, and Tan (2000), and Hoff and Bashir (2015)). Thus, both are closely related and linked to each other. The reason why both constructs experience high interest is their shared consequence: improved performance for a task at hand, which is an economically measurable value (Siau and Wang 2018; Honeycutt, Nourani, and Ragan 2020; Nam et al. 2020).

The second question concerning the difference between trust in humans and trust in technology emerged as technology turned from a mere mediator of trust between humans, to the trustee itself (Sollner € and Pavlou 2016). Initially, researchers simply transferred the concepts of human-human trust to humanmachine trust. For example, Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman (1995) widely accepted three dimensions of trust: ability, benevolence, and integrity (see e. g. Schmidt, Biessmann, and Teubner (2020), Glikson and Woolley (2020), Rousseau et al. (1998), Sollner € et al. (2012)). While some argued that this interpersonal foundation is applicable for research in humanmachine trust (Benbasat and Wang 2005), others created new dimensions, like performance, process, and purpose (Lee and See 2004) or performance, helpfulness, and predictability (Sollner € and Pavlou 2016). This separation is often justified by contrasting Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman (1995) dimensions for humanhuman trust with Lee and See’s (2004) dimensions for human-machine trust (see e. g. Sollner € and Pavlou (2016) or Asan, Bayrak, and Choudhury (2020)). Surprisingly, recent research employed these two references to justify the exact opposite because neither Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman (1995) nor Lee and See (2004) restricted their definition of trust to either human-human or human-machine trust (see Daronnat (2020), Glikson and Woolley (2020), or Schmidt, Biessmann, and Teubner (2020)). This perspective is supported by the computers as social actors (CASA) paradigm (Nass and Moon 2000). Nass and Moon (2000) suggest that humans automatically behave in a social manner even when interacting with a machine and being aware of this (see also Nass et al. (1995) and Nass, Fogg, and Moon (1996)). In this sense, trust in machines would be a mere spill-over effect, an overgeneralisation. Therefore, it remains debateable whether principles of human-human trust may be directly transferable to human-machine trust (Rheu et al. 2020).

Here, we want to emphasise that this may be right for traditional technology, considered as a tool, but should be reconsidered in light of new technology, like AI. AI is different from previous technology: autonomous instead of automatic (de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018; Bigman et al. 2019). Along with this, “AI can behave proactively, unexpectedly, and incomprehensibly for humans” (Saßmannshausen et al. 2021, p. 1333) and thus implies a counterpart, albeit technological, which nevertheless invites social interaction (Hassenzahl et al. 2021). This new class of technology is not experienced as a tool-like extension of human abilities and strictly speaking, is not used by humans. Instead, humans are in dialog with this technology – they delegate and cooperate – which turns it into an active, socially experienced counterpart (Hassenzahl et al. 2021). For Hassenzahl et al. (2021) these new qualities warrant a new terminology to clearly distinguish “traditional,” tool-like, passive technology from, what they call, otherware. Exemplary representations of otherware are “chatbots, smart home devices, self-driving cars, or autonomous robots” (Hassenzahl et al. 2021, p. 54). All these systems invite and rely on a form of human-technology relationship, which is fundamentally social.

While most design approaches aim to make the technology “disappear” when in use (view of technology as an unperceived tool-like extension) (Hassenzahl et al. 2021), this new class of technology defies this approach per definition (view of technology as a perceived social counterpart). Consequently, it requires a new design approach to establish productive and humane cooperation with otherware (Norman, Ortony, and Russell 2003; Haslam 2006; Riedl 2019; Hassenzahl et al. 2021; Shneiderman 2020).

Regarding trust, we observe the tendency to question the antecedents from research in “old-fashioned technology” (Sullivan, de Bourmont, and Dunaway 2022) and increasingly rely on antecedents from interpersonal trust research (de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018). We believe that the truth is – as often – somewhere in between, as this new technology is somewhat other than previous technologies, but also other than humans. Hence, we support the verification and, if necessary, revision of existing trust antecedents in light of this new technology (Detweiler and Broekens 2009; Farooq and Grudin 2016). To serve this approach, we aim to create a comprehensive map of researched trust antecedents in technology perceived as a counterpart (otherware).

## Methodological review procedure

In order to get a broad overview of antecedents of trust in all forms of technology-based counterparts, we conducted an extensive and systematic literature search and review. Our methodology followed the five steps of vom Brocke et al. (2009): (1) definition of the review scope, (2) conceptualisation of the topic, (3) search for literature, (4) analysis and synthesis of literature, and (5) deduction of future research. Within the first four steps, further established methods were applied to ensure comprehensibility, transparency, and reproducibility.

## Scope definition

We characterised the review using the taxonomy of Cooper (1988) and broadened it by the review type defined by Par�e et al. (2015), see Figure 1. Our focus was on research outcomes and theories with the goal to integrate them from a neutral perspective. Therefore, we organised the review as exhaustive and selective, as well as conceptual. Our target groups are specialised disciplines, like human factors, human-computer interaction, human-robot interaction, systems engineering, information systems (IS) research, and collaboration engineering. Summing up, the review processed a theoretical scoping on antecedents of trust in relationships between human and technology-based counterparts. Thereby, we aim to promote further research and want to answer the following research questions (RQ).

� RQ1: Is there a representative definition of trust for the interaction of humans and otherware that is mostly employed by the research community?

� RQ2: What are existing trust antecedents in human-otherware relationships and how can they be structured?

## Conceptualisation and search

Torraco (2005) strongly recommends the acquisition of a priori knowledge as essential to conduct a highquality review. For this purpose, we reviewed over 40 publications in an exploratory manner, as well as to facilitate the construction of an appropriate search string. This resulted in the following search string, including Boolean operators and wildcards: (“trust” OR “trustworth�”) AND (“technolog�” OR “robot�” OR “machine�” OR “automation�” OR “autonomy�” OR “agent�” OR “IT system�” OR “IT artifact�” OR “artificial intelligence” OR “machine learning”). The wildcard operator (�) serves to avoid distinct formulations, e. g. noun, verb, and adjective.

To objectify the subsequent search we employed the eight elements of the STARLITE mnemonic framework (Booth 2006). The sampling strategy was in line with the review scope and aimed to identify all relevant studies. Therefore, we did not narrow the type of studies or the inclusions and exclusions terms for further filtering. The year of publication was limited to 2020 as the upper limit to include only whole years. As limitation, we only considered publications written in English. The approach was an electronic search in the following 13 databases (sources): ACM Digital Library, Business Source Complete, EBSCO Host, Emerald Insight, IEEE Xplore, JSTOR, ProQuest, PsycARTICLES, Psychology and Behavioural Science Collection, PsycINFO, PSYNEX, Science Direct, and Web of Science. The employment of the search string in these databases (title only) resulted in a total of 3,358 publications.

## Reduction and analysis

For the stepwise reduction of the identified 3,358 publications, we employed the procedure given in the PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al. 2009). First, we excluded the duplicates yielding to 1,531 remaining publications. Second, we utilised the text clustering approach recommended by Weißer et al. (2020) on the publication titles. This algorithmic supported reduction approach is based on natural language processing (NLP). That in details means, tokenization of the words in the considered publications, removal of stop words (common words like articles, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, that carry no information), TFIDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) vectorisation as a relative metric for the relevance of a word, and k-Means clustering to group publications with similarity in content. To determine the number of clusters we employed the elbow method (Ketchen, Jr. and Shook 1996). This led to a number of 20 clusters, that are characterised by intrahomogeneity and inter-heterogeneity (Wright 1974), so that the top words (most relevant terms per cluster) describe the thematical focus of the whole cluster, see Table 1.

Thus, we aimed to exclude/include whole clusters by applying the two quality criteria (QC) on the top words as well as on a random sample of abstracts of each cluster.

� QC1: Publications address the interaction, cooperation, or collaboration of humans with technology

� QC2: Within this human-otherware relationships the publications focus on human trust and examine at least one antecedent of human trust.

Here, four clusters with a total number of 493 publications fulfilled all quality criteria – interestingly, all four have human or humanoid as one top word. In the next (third) reduction step, we manually screened the abstracts with two independent researchers, leading to 250 publications that fulfilled our quality criteria.

Out of these 250 publications, 179 passed the last step, the full-text screening, and were considered for further analysis and synthesis. Figure 2 summarises all reduction steps and the 179 identified publications are listed online at Mendeley Data, see Saßmannshausen (2022).

## Descriptive synthesis

Table 2 shows the chronology of the publication corpus, separated per terminology used for the technology-based counterpart. Since 2015 we observe a rise in the number of publications with a dramatic increase in 2020, underlining the relevance of trust research in this new type of intelligent technology. While the term automation has been used consistently over time, the usage of robot for a technology-based counterpart had its breakthrough in 2016. A little later, in 2018, the term artificial intelligence – including machine learning – came in and is quite emergent. Parallel to these three main terms, some authors employ terms like agent, artefact, chatbot, machine, or avatar, which are aggregated into other.

Most of the identified publications do not focus on a specific application (99 of 179) but examine the trust relationship between humans and otherware in general. Looking at the application areas in Table 3, we notice that safety-critical applications are of higher interest, such as autonomous driving, military systems, as well as airport and aircraft security. In these areas, the term automation seems to be popular. The robot is the favourite counterpart in the areas of home care (especially for elderly people), emergency rescue, production (especially assembly tasks), and education. It seems that in these applications a form of physical representation (i. e., a body) tends to be essential. In comparison, the areas of health care and data science appear not to require a physical representation, resulting in the term artificial intelligence. Given the diversity of application areas and terms for technology-based counterparts, the sample is a good foundation for answering our research questions.

## Discussion of trust definition

To answer our first research question and build on the earlier discussion of trust definitions, we analysed our sample of 179 publications with respect to a representative definition of trust for the interaction of humans and otherware. Eighty-five (85) publications do not contain any definition of trust. This seems to mirror the finding of Biros, Daly, and Gunsch (2004) that most authors do not define trust, assuming it is a well-known concept already. Whereas trust was first defined for interpersonal relationships (e. g. Deutsch (1962), Luhmann (1979)) it was later transferred to human-machine relationships (Lee and Moray 1994; Muir 1994). Apparently, there is some confusion about how to define trust in this research stream (Walterbusch et al. 2014; Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2018), resulting in 15 self-created definitions and 22 definitions of low citation frequency (smaller or equal to three). There are only two, widely cited definitions:

� Lee and See (2004, p. 51): Trust is “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” (35 citations).

� Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman (1995, p. 712): Trust is “the willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party based on the expectation that the other will perform a particular action important to the trustor, irrespective of the ability to monitor or control that other part” (20 citations).

While the definition of Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman (1995) transfers notions of human-human trust onto human-otherware trust, the one of Lee and See (2004) is especially focussed on, but not limited to, human-otherware trust. Both definitions do not exclude each other, which is underlined by their combined utilisation in four identified publications (see Korber, € Baseler, and Bengler (2018), Abbass (2019), Asan, Bayrak, and Choudhury (2020), and Thiebes, Lins, and Sunyaev (2021)). Neither definition limits one side – trustor or trustee – to be either a human being or an otherware. As we see it, these definitions harmonise well. They have in common that there must be some task for whose execution the trustor needs the trustee. If the trustee’s execution is uncertain the trustor becomes vulnerable. If the trustor accepts this vulnerability, then he/she trusts the trustee.

We have shown that there are (at least two) sound, generic, and inclusive trust definitions. Therefore, the revealed practice of not using a definition is even more questionable. Even though trust is a well-known concept, we recommend the use of a definition, in the spirit of good research practice. For our second research question, we nevertheless considered the publications without a definition because they contain valuable insights on trust antecedents.

## Discussion of trust antecedents

To answer our second research question, we screened all 179 resulting publications for antecedents of trust. While some of the publications just revealed one ante cedent, others uncovered multiple antecedents. After extracting the antecedents and harmonising the used terminology we revealed a sum of 479 different antecedents. On a superordinate level, it seems that there is a consensus on three groups for classification: (1) antecedents of the environment (situation or context); (2) antecedents of the trustor (human); and (3) antecedents of the trustee (otherware, automation, robot, AI, or technology). These three groups emerged from conceptual clustering of empirical studies (e. g. Wagner, Robinette, and Howard (2018), Saßmannshausen et al. (2021)) as well as from literature reviews and metaanalyses (e. g. Hancock et al. (2011), Schaefer et al. (2016), Siau and Wang (2018)). Hoff and Bashir (2013, 2015) mapped these three groups to the three trust layers of Marsh & Dibben (2005): Here, the environmental antecedents influence the situational trust, whereas the trustor antecedents affect the dispositional trust, and the trustee antecedents impact the learned trust. Inspired by the division of the last layer, learned trust, into initial learned trust (prior to interaction) and dynamic learned trust (during interaction) (Hoff and Bashir 2015) we strongly recommend establishing four groups of trust antecedents – namely the environment (also situation or context), the human as trustor, the otherware as trustee (also automation, robot, AI, or other terms for technology-based counterparts), and as a new group the interaction. The new fourth group, interaction, reflects the dynamic learned trust and enables the integration of research antecedents that have not yet been integrated, such as the antecedents of trust repair (Dai and Wu 2015).

Within these four groups, we employed a hierarchical structure with multiple levels to provide a better overview. For example within the group otherware (trustee), some publications identified the anthropomorphic appearance as one antecedent (level 1), while others refer to a special detail of it – the facial appearance – as one antecedent (level 2), and still others went further into detail and examined the brownnose-chin ratio as one antecedent (level 3). To be clear, for our understanding, these are all antecedents of trust, but at different levels of detail.

In Figure 3 we visualised all 479 antecedents – using the software Gephi (Bastian, Heymann, and Jacomy 2009) – according to the described grouping and structuring. As it can be seen, the otherware group covers nearly half of the hierarchical network (228 antecedents). The other groups have noticeably fewer antecedents: human (94), interaction (93), and environment (64). A list of all antecedents can be found in the Appendix. Furthermore, all data and graphic files are available online at Mendeley Data, see Saßmannshausen (2022). In the following, we will discuss the three most relevant level 1 antecedents per group. Here, the relevance is assessed by the number of publications dealing with the corresponding antecedents.

## Trust antecedents of the environment

Lee and See (2004, p. 56) stated “Trust does not develop in a vacuum but, instead, evolves in a complex individual, cultural, and organizational context.” Thus, the environment group describes all trust antecedents that are external to the trustor, trustee, and their interaction. It is covered by 58 of the 179 publications and contains 64 antecedents of different levels. Table 4 shows the level 1 antecedents and qualifies them according to their corresponding number of sub-antecedents and the number of publications covering all three levels – the sources for the antecedents can be found online at Mendeley Data, see Saßmannshausen (2022). Subsequently, we discuss a selection of the level 1 antecedents (highlighted in bold).

For the level 1 antecedent task, the complexity and the difficulty are central. While some results indicate that simpler tasks (lower difficulty) go along with higher trust (Bitkina et al. 2020) others show the opposite (Deligianis et al. 2017). Thus, the antecedent workload is often regarded instead. The workload increases with higher task difficulty and additional tasks (multi-tasking), leading to higher trust (Biros, Daly, and Gunsch 2004). As a high workload causes higher stress and thus can reduce performance (Ding et al. 2020; Peruzzini, Grandi, and Pellicciari 2020) this trust is likely to be misplaced overtrust (Parasuraman, Molloy, and Singh 1993) as an attempt to keep performance up.

The effect of a high workload interacts with the risk of the situation (Sato et al. 2020). Here, it is noteworthy that most researchers examine subjectively perceived risk rather than objectively defined risk (Pinto et al. 2020; Saßmannshausen et al. 2021).

While Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018) point out that higher perceived risk leads to reduced willingness to interact with and trust the otherware, Sato et al. (2020) elaborated that in high workload situations, a higher risk is accompanied by higher trust. A similar result is reported by Robinette, Howard, and Wagner (2017), with the difference that users follow the otherware due to a workload-enforced reliance rather than trust. While in these studies the distinction between trust and reliance is very transparent, we will highlight studies that mean trust but say reliance, or say trust but measure reliance. Coming back to the antecedent of risk, the result seems to be that high risk is related to lower trust in some settings and to higher trust in others, requiring further research on antecedent interactions.

The level 1 antecedent team describes the social setting of the trustee, e. g. human colleagues, and superiors. Here, the team configuration, also called composition, plays an important role (Yagoda and Gillan 2012; Schaefer et al. 2016; Hancock et al. 2021). It determines the team’s size, diversity, and roles, which in turn affect the team and individual performance and trust in each other (Hoff and Bashir 2015; McNeese et al. 2019). In addition, team members share positive/neutral/negative attitudes (Volante et al. 2019), mental models (Hancock et al. 2011), and knowledge (Christensen and Lyons 2017) concerning the otherware.

## Trust antecedents of the human

Our trust map (Figure 3) emphasises what Baker et al. (2018) observed: there are many efforts to identify and understand the antecedents of the otherware, while the human antecedents seem to be underrepresented. An assumption for this trend may be that most research focuses on the antecedents that can be influenced in terms of technology design. Table 5 presents the level 1 antecedents of the human group, which contains 94 antecedents in total and is covered by 74 publications.

The most popular level 1 antecedent is the one for the human characteristics, ranging from a general propensity to trust (Merritt et al. 2013) and interact (Qin, Li, and Yan 2020), over risk aversion (Hass 2020) and tolerance (Brown 2020), to attitudes on (Tussyadiah, Zach, and Wang 2020) and comfort with (Xie et al. 2020) otherware. Within the human characteristics, the personality stands out as the most prominent level 2 antecedent. It is mostly operationalised with the established psychological model “Big Five,” which uses five personality traits to describe a personality – namely openness, extraversion, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (here regarded as level 3 antecedents) (Hass 2020; Oksanen et al. 2020; Sharan and Romano 2020; Zhou, Luo, and Chen 2020). Even though the findings indicate inconsistent relationships between these five traits and trust (Hass 2020; Sharan and Romano 2020), a tendency can be identified: low openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion as well as high agreeableness and neuroticism coincide with higher levels of trust (Zhou, Luo, and Chen 2020).

Regarding the level 1 antecedent experience, an extended positive interaction history – even indirectly through experiences of others (Lee and See 2004) – fosters trust (Deutsch 1958; Muir 1987, 1994). The main reason is probably that experienced people are able to adjust their expectations adequately (Sollner € and Pavlou 2016). This increases the chance of congruence of expectation and observation, which likewise increases trust. However, the adjustment of expectation might be biased by other antecedents, such as the appearance of the otherware (see next chapter). Similarly, the observation can be influenced. For instance, if malfunctions never become transparent to the human, he/she perceives the performance to be higher than it actually is. The assumption, however, is that as experience increases, these biases will be perceived, reflected, and integrated into the formation of accurate expectations.

This is different from the human’s experience to solve the task at hand, here named level 1 antecedent ability (also called capability, competence, skill, or expertise). Higher abilities for the task lead to lower trust, whereas lower abilities lead to higher trust (Hoff and Bashir 2015). This can be interpreted as an indication that a subject matter expert claims expert status for himself. In contrast, a novice human seems to be more open about getting assistance from otherware. But this relationship could also be influenced by the subjectively perceived workload or risk. A novice has a weak ability for the task at hand and thus is likely to experience a higher workload and might be unable to correctly assess the risk. Thus, the difference in trust between novices and experts could also be due to the different subjective perceptions of the task and situation antecedents (see the previous chapter).

The level 1 antecedent mental states is a kind of collector for different level 2 antecedents, such as the willingness or motivation to cooperate (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2018) and the current stress level or fatigue of the human (Schaefer et al. 2016). Here, the direction of the influence on the trust (positive or negative) is as one would expect, e. g. the more motivated or willing a person is to cooperate the greater the trust.

Underneath the level 1 antecedent demographics, the human’s age and gender are most researched. While some studies do not find a significant influence of age on trust (Swanson, Bellanca, and Helton 2019) others found that e. g. seven-year-old children trust a robot for playing more than younger children (Di Dio et al. 2020). In addition, elderly people tend to trust more when dealing with healthcare robots (Fischer, Weigelin, and Bodenhagen 2018). Here, older people may be more forgiving of malfunctions than young people, possibly because of their dependence on the technology (de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018). On the other hand, age might be related to digital affinity, which in turn fosters trust (Saßmannshausen et al. 2021). Regarding the human gender, there is a serious influence through the interaction with the gender attributed to the otherware: Men trust otherware with a female voice less than women do (Wong, Xu, and Dudek 2019).

## Trust antecedents of the otherware

We extracted 228 antecedents out of 141 publications for the otherware group. Table 6 illustrates the identified level 1 antecedents of the otherware. In this respect, literature repeatedly highlights performance as a key indicator of trust (Baker et al. 2018) – also compared to antecedents of other groups.

The level 1 antecedent performance is also referred to as ability, accuracy, capability, competency, expertise, and experience of the otherware to complete the task at hand or to assist the human to do so (McKnight et al. 2011). To avoid over- and undertrust, proper calibration of the human to the otherware’s performance is essential. Here, the otherware’s reliability is an important (level 2) antecedent (Parasuraman, Molloy, and Singh 1993; Parasuraman and Riley 1997). Normally, high reliability equals high trust, but as Baker et al. (2018) point out, this is not always the case. If high reliability causes decreasing situation awareness of the human or a stronger task allocation to the otherware, the ability of humans to accurately take over from the otherware in case of an error is also decreasing. Thus, unexpected errors and failures ought to be prevented (Siau and Wang 2018). While there are a lot of different failure types (Hoff and Bashir 2015), they can be separated into two categories. Chronic errors (first category) steadily erode performance, and acute errors (second category) are followed by a direct and often massive decrease in performance, which, however, restores to the former level after the error has been corrected (Lee and Moray 1992; Lee and See 2004). After an error, trust declines, not instantly but over time, and its recovery behaves similarly (de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018). Here, the magnitude of the trust change over time varies from human to human (Lee and Moray 1994; Lee and See 2004).

To additionally support trust-building, the otherware should be predictable to the human (Culley and Madhavan 2013; Balfe, Sharples, and Wilson 2018). Therefore, its processes, e. g. data management (Qin, Li, and Yan 2020), should be robust (Asan, Bayrak, and Choudhury 2020), persistent (Muir 1987, 1994), and consistent (Stuck and Rogers 2018). Going a step further the level 1 antecedent explainability has become a focus topic in research, fuelled by the successes of incomprehensible deep neural networks in Atari games (Mnih et al. 2013; Mnih et al. 2015). Here, context-dependent transparency supports the understanding of the otherware and thus the proper trust calibration (Chen and Barnes 2014; Boyce et al. 2015; Baker et al. 2018). Yet it is an open question which level of transparency is required (de Visser et al. 2014; Morita and Burns 2014) and which effects are produced by different forms of transparency (Baker et al. 2018). While transparency is a passive state of explainability, it can be enriched by active explanations of the otherware, for example, the communication of reasons for a specific outcome or an error (Boyce et al. 2015). What constitutes a sound explanation from a human factors perspective is an open research question (Riedl 2019). Sanneman and Shah (2020), for example, examined performance-, process-, and purpose-based explanations. However, since explanations are generated post-hoc, humans tend to create plausible descriptions to justify their behaviour or choices – they invent a consistent story because they do not understand neurological reasoning (Riedl 2019). Initial attempts with these human-like explanations instead of the more prominent approach to “open the black box” processes reveal promising results for trustbuilding (Ehsan et al. 2019). From a philosophical perspective (Gabriel 2012), this is the question of explanations regarding validity (justification) or genesis (formation) of otherware’s decisions.

As research shows, trust does not only depend on technical features that reflect the otherware’s performance or explainability but also on its appearance. Whether virtual or physical representation, appearance plays an important role in trust-building (Baker et al. 2018). Especially for initial trust-building, familiar appearances similar to humans or animals are used to connect on an emotional level (Siau and Wang 2018). This anthropomorphism is not restricted to appearance, other human-like features range from politeness and etiquette (Parasuraman and Miller 2004), over face features (Song and Luximon 2020), to cognitive similarity (de Visser et al. 2012). In terms of trust, anthropomorphism is a solid approach, as long as the similarity is not too high. If so, the Uncanny Valley effect emerges, indicating a negative impact on the interaction (Mori, MacDorman, and Kageki 2012). To overcome this and other issues occurring from strong anthropomorphism (and zoomorphism) Hassenzahl et al. (2021) recommend treating otherware as a “third species,” which should be designed as such but should also retain the benefits of fundamentally social interaction (Laschke et al. 2020).

## Trust antecedents of the interaction

The interaction between human and otherware is highly dynamic, leading to nonlinear changes in trust: “Negative interactions have a greater influence than do positive interactions” (Lee and See (2004, p. 72) after Kramer (1999)). To better deal with the negative interactions, we discovered extensive research on trust repair, which had not yet been part of trust models describing trust antecedents (see Hancock et al. (2011), Hoff and Bashir (2015), Schaefer et al. (2016), Siau and Wang (2018), Hancock et al. (2021)). Out of 40 publications dealing with the interaction, we revealed 93 antecedents. Table 7 demonstrates all level 1 antecedents with their respective metrics.

The level 1 antecedent adaption deals e. g. with the dynamic adjustment of the otherware’s behaviour (Xu and Dudek 2015), transparency (Akash et al. 2020), position relative to the human (Fischer, Weigelin, and Bodenhagen 2018), or task allocation (Lewandowsky, Mundy, and Tan 2000; Abbass 2019). The goal is to improve the overall performance by utilising complementary strengths, based on the current states of the human and otherware (Lu et al. 2021). In doing so, we overcome the a priori (static) division of labour, also known as MABA-MABA (men-are-better-at/machinesare-better-at) (Dekker and Woods 2002). Within the discussion of designing adaption there are two streams: prepare the otherware to initiate adjustments by itself – adapting – or to be adjustable by the human – adaptable. For adapting otherware, the human state has to be monitored and considered in the otherware’s decision process, like other environmental influences (Christensen and Lyons 2017). To enable appropriate trust, the human should understand how the otherware will change. To do so it is important to always keep the human involved (in the loop), albeit only at a minimal (Ullman and Malle 2017), to gain interaction experience. In contrast, adaptable otherware gives control to the human, which is more likely to meet Rosenbrock’s (1990) as well as de Winter, Hancock, and de Winter (2021) postulation for technology that serves humans. One challenge for future research will be that humans need to understand when to take control (Baker et al. 2018). This will cause a shift in human activities, with a stronger focus on monitoring (Dellermann et al. 2019).

Adapting is also important within the verbal interaction, here called communication. Interaction designers could vary several speech parameters to influence trust, like information density, rate, and complexity (Hancock, Stowers, and Kessler 2019) or intonation and frequency range (Nass and Lee 2001). The purpose is to create a pleasant atmosphere for the human, taking into account not only the content (Stuck and Rogers 2018; Hashemian et al. 2019) but also non-verbal communication (Arts et al. 2020; Rheu et al. 2020).

The next level 1 antecedent deals with the repair methods, which – as well as dampening methods – can be employed by the otherware to ensure proper trust calibration Here, the repair methods gained more research interest, indicating that undertrust seems to be a more common or more relevant problem than overtrust. In addition, repair methods are often applied after trust violations, such as errors or failures, wherein the most popular repair methods are apologising, explaining, promising to do better as well as denying and blaming someone/something else (de Visser, Pak, and Shaw 2018; de Visser et al. 2019; Sebo, Krishnamurthi, and Scassellati 2019; Tolmeijer et al. 2020).

## Limitations and future research

Our remarks emphasise that trust relationships change dynamically over time (Hoff and Bashir 2015; Daronnat 2020) and are influenced by multifaceted antecedents and their complex interplay (Drnec et al. 2016; Baker et al. 2018). Previous research suggests that trust is quite stable when it depends on multiple antecedents (McKnight, Cummings, and Chervany 1998; Lee and

See 2004). Thus, future research can build on our trust map (see Figure 3 and for full details see Appendix) and identify which antecedents and combinations of antecedents lead to a robust trust state. As an example of an interaction effect between culture (human) and appearance (otherware), the work of Lee and Sabanovi�c (2014) can be cited. They found that people from South Korea and Turkey prefer robots appearing life-like with facial expressions, while those from the U.S. choose machine-like robots. However, it might be not just the culture, but the things the culture is driving that end up making appearance matter. Cultures that value robots for security and safety applications could develop more machine-like robots than cultures that value robots for elder- and healthcare applications, which in turn could produce more human-like robots. We want to emphasise that the relationship between two antecedents may be more complex than initially assumed. We, therefore, encourage future research to explore antecedents and interactions in greater depth.

Moreover, the identified 479 trust antecedents could be assigned to the phases of the trust lifecycle developed by Sollner € and Pavlou (2016) based on the initial work of Rousseau et al. (1998). Figure 4 illustrates the trust lifecycle with an exemplary assignment of antecedents to the phases. While, for example, the characteristics of the human determine trust before the first interaction, this may be confirmed (or corrected) by the otherware’s appearance during the first interaction. In ongoing interaction, features such as good explainability may increase trust, and appropriate adaptation modes may maintain it at a stable level. In contrast, decreasing performance leads to a loss of trust, which can be mitigated by appropriate repair methods, such as an apology.

As Baker et al. (2018, p. 9) stated, humans interact with otherware bearing all their subjective “notions, fears, and experiences” which affect the gain and loss of trust. As a result, some researchers argue that the antecedents of the groups environment and otherware should not be regarded as objective. Instead, human perceptions of these antecedents should be treated as influencing the trust, like perceived difficulty of the task or perceived competence of the otherware (Merritt and Ilgen 2008; Bitkina et al. 2020; Saßmannshausen et al. 2021). We believe this is implicitly the case because of the 179 identified publications 111 were experiments and most of them with self-reporting scales as measurement method. We encourage future research to evaluate for which antecedents an objective metric adequately describes the effect on trust and for which antecedents the human’s subjective perceptions should be considered. This will serve designers and engineers to create more trustful human-otherware teams as well as to better calibrate and maintain human trust.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 4. Trust lifecycle according to S€ollner and Pavlou (2016) extended by exemplary antecedents per phase.

Beyond the question of objective vs. subjective measurement, there is also the question of whether the trust has actually been measured. In our introduction, we already addressed the distinction between trust and reliance. In some studies, this distinction does not seem to exist (consciously or unconsciously), resulting in studies meaning trust but saying reliance or saying trust but measuring reliance, or vice versa. With such use, misunderstandings and misleading interpretations are inevitable. We intend to raise the awareness of future research for the correct terminological use and measurement of trust.

## Critical reflection

Our discussion of the key antecedents provided a glimpse of the complexity of determining trust. In doing so, we have limited the discussion to a few antecedents and interactions between them. On this basis, it is easy to imagine the incredible complexity of a system consisting of all 479 antecedents with multiple interactions. Think of a prediction model, e. g. a regression model, with only a fraction of these antecedents as parameters. It is highly questionable whether such a model would work adequately at all, or whether it would be used at all. It would be very complicated, confusing, and difficult to understand for predicting trust. This raises the question of whether the current research practice is purposeful. In order to explain this perspective, we return to the expressed goal of trust research in human-otherware interaction: the proper calibration of human trust. So it is about actively calibrating trust – managing it, controlling it. The research path taken so far seems to be in the spirit of Ashby (1964). He states that a controlling system must have at least the same complexity as the system to be controlled. Here, we do not know the complexity of the system to be controlled (trust), but let us assume that it is high, very high. Given this assumption, it is not surprising that various research papers keep uncovering new antecedents as “buttons” to the control panel of trust. Currently, research seems focussed on answering the question “What happens to trust when we push this or that (new) button?” Thus, the control panel grows larger and larger – new terms are steadily added to the list of antecedents. The present paper makes it even worse by adding a whole group of 93 antecedents, the interaction group. In doing so, we aimed to mirror and exaggerate the current research practice. We believe if research sticks to this practice, more and more antecedents will be added without providing a better understanding of trust or how to design real-world applications for trust.

Therefore, we would like to encourage future research to refrain from the existing practice of empirically exploring new antecedents or reorganising existing antecedents reviewer-wise. Instead, we propose to explore the underlying, deeper operating mechanisms of antecedents and their interactions: How do antecedents affect the trust, the way they do?

## Conclusion

By answering our research questions, we showed that trust in intelligent technology-based counterparts – or trust in otherware as we call it – is more than the current ethics-driven discussions on “Trustworthy AI” suggest. To the best of our knowledge, the presented analysis is the most exhaustive one, which revealed 479 antecedents influencing human trust in otherware. By structuring this immense number of antecedents, we identified four groups – environment, human, otherware, and interaction – and have thus extended the usual threefold model by the fourth group, the interaction.

This enabled us to include research on trust repair, which had not been integrated before. In conclusion, we created a comprehensive map of trust antecedents. At the same time, we questioned the usefulness of this research practice of “more and more antecedents” and recommend trust research that uncovers the deeper trust mechanisms. We advocate for technology development with human trust in mind. In doing so, we join the repeating and alternating cycles of pure technology development and the subsequent design for its usage by or interaction with humans (Grudin 2009). In the upcoming decades, humancentered design and especially trust will become even more decisive. First, following Huang, Rust, and Maksimovic (2019) we are facing an economy change: from thinking to feeling. Decisions are increasingly made based on feelings, including whether or not to interact with otherware. Second, given the development towards artificial general intelligence (AGI) and Alfonseca et al.’s (2021) proof that humans will not be able to control it, interaction will have to rely more on trust.
